summary: Mn-35 is the highest-manganese member of the Fe(x)Mn11Al1C low-density steel series (nominal 35Mn–11Al–1C), studied in the as-solution-treated condition (1050 °C/2 h followed by water quenching) after vacuum induction melting, homogenization and hot rolling. It is a single-phase FCC austenitic low-density steel (density 6.53 g/cm³) containing uniformly dispersed, coherent nano-scale κ-carbides (~2 nm) and abundant Σ3 twin boundaries. It is the softest and most ductile grade of the series, and serves as the key composition for understanding how Mn content alters κ-carbide size and thereby strength, work-hardening and toughness.
composition: The alloy belongs to the Fe(x)Mn11Al1C series (nominally 11 wt% Al, 1 wt% C, with Mn varied from 20 to 35 wt%) and is designated Mn-35. Its measured chemical composition is 34.23 wt% Mn, 11.10 wt% Al, 1.00 wt% C, with Fe as the balance (Table 1). The design places it at the upper end of the Mn range explored: the high Mn addition (34.23%) strongly stabilizes the austenite so that no ferrite remains, while C and Al provide solid-solution strengthening and the lightweight character of these low-density steels (Al and C being the light, lattice-expanding additions). Al and C are also the elements that promote κ-carbide precipitation, whereas Mn acts to inhibit κ-carbide formation and growth — so this composition combines strong austenite stability with the finest κ-carbide population of the series. Its experimental density is 6.53 g/cm³, consistent with the alloy's overall relation ρ = 8.1 − 0.102C − 0.10Al − 0.01Mn (mass%).
processing: The processing lineage starts with melting and casting: the steel was melted in a high-frequency vacuum induction furnace (50 kg capacity, vacuum atmosphere) and cast into a 150 mm diameter ingot. The ingot was then homogenized at 1200 °C for 5 h and hot rolled into 16 mm diameter rods, which were air-cooled to room temperature (the parent hot-rolled state). The final, studied state is a solution treatment: the hot-rolled rod was held at 1050 °C for 2 h and then water quenched. This 1050 °C–2 h–WQ condition is the terminal state used for tensile testing, Charpy impact testing, density measurement and the EBSD/TEM microstructural characterization.
microstructure: After solution treatment at 1050 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching, the Mn-35 steel is fully austenitic: EBSD shows a single FCC austenite phase with no ferrite (ferrite fraction listed as "-"), i.e. the 35% Mn addition is sufficient to suppress the BCC phase entirely. The austenite is equiaxed with a coarse average grain size of 33 ± 1.6 μm — the coarsest of the Mn series and consistent with the general trend that raising Mn dissolves ferrite and allows austenite grains to coarsen (9.9 μm at 20% Mn → 33 μm at 35% Mn). The grains contain abundant Σ3 twin boundaries, with a twin-boundary fraction f_Tw of 59.6% (about 60%), essentially unchanged with grain coarsening. The microstructure carries a uniform dispersion of nano-scale κ-carbides of average size 2.0 ± 1.1 nm — the finest κ-carbide population measured across all levels of the C, Mn and Al series. SAED confirms a coherent γ/κ orientation relationship of (001)κ || (001)γ, i.e. the κ-carbides are coherent with the austenite matrix. The κ-carbides originate from spinodal decomposition and ordering of C and Al in the austenite, and their refinement with increasing Mn (5 nm at 25% Mn down to 2 nm at 35% Mn) reflects the inhibiting effect of Mn on κ-carbide precipitation and coarsening.
properties: Tensile and impact testing was performed on two solution-treated specimens (data reported as averages) with the tensile axis parallel to the rod axis (gauge length 25 mm, diameter 5 mm), an initial strain rate of 1.1 × 10^-3 s^-1 at ambient temperature, and Charpy V-notch specimens with the notch perpendicular to the rod axis tested at −40 °C. The mechanical properties of Mn-35 in the 1050 °C/2 h + WQ state are: yield strength 401 ± 5 MPa, ultimate tensile strength 849 ± 1 MPa, uniform elongation 60 ± 0.4%, total elongation to failure 75.0 ± 1%. Supplementary stress measures derived from the curves are σ_TS (maximum true stress just before necking/crack nucleation) = 1313 MPa and σ_FS (fracture strength) = 2200 MPa. Its maximum work-hardening rate, ~2300 MPa, is the highest of the Mn series. Charpy V-notch impact energy at −40 °C is 19.3 ± 2.1 J. The density measured by the Archimedes drainage method is 6.53 g/cm³. Characterization techniques applied to this sample were EBSD (FEG-SEM FEI Quanta 650, 20 kV, 0.5 μm step, 7% Nital electro-polishing, grain size by linear intercept with a 15° boundary definition, Channel 5 software), TEM dark-field imaging with SAED (Tecnai G2 F20 S-TWIN, 200 kV, twin-jet electro-polished foils in 10% perchloric acid/90% ethanol at 20 V and −20 °C, imaged along [001]γ using a κ-carbide reflection), Archimedes density measurement, uniaxial tensile testing (MTS machine) and Charpy impact testing (MTS impact tester, 500 J capacity). Across the Fe(x)Mn11Al1C series, increasing Mn from 20% to 35% lowers yield strength from 896 MPa to 401 MPa while total elongation rises from 28.5% to 60% and the work-hardening rate increases; the Mn-35 grade is therefore the softest and most ductile of the series.
mechanisms: Increasing Mn content stabilizes austenite and suppresses ferrite: at 20% Mn a small ferrite fraction (3.30%) remains and at 25% Mn it drops to 0.65%, so by 35% Mn the microstructure is single-phase austenite — the ferrite bands that pin/refine austenite grains are eliminated and the austenite grains coarsen from 9.9 μm (20% Mn) to 33 μm (35% Mn).

Mn inhibits κ-carbide precipitation and coarsening, so the average κ-carbide diameter shrinks monotonically with Mn content (18 nm at 20% Mn → 5 nm at 25% Mn → 3 nm at 30% Mn → 2.0 nm at 35% Mn), producing the finest carbide dispersion of the series.

κ-carbides strengthen the austenite by a particle-shear mechanism rather than Orowan bypassing, because SAED shows a coherent (001)κ || (001)γ interface; the shear-strength contribution follows σ_shear = α f^1/2 d_Car^1/2, giving a linear yield-strength dependence on the square root of carbide size with a slope of 97.1 MPa/nm^1/2, while the carbide-free flow stress is about 478 MPa (from solid-solution and grain-size strengthening).

Because carbide size controls strength, the finest κ-carbides (2 nm) in Mn-35 give the lowest yield strength (401 MPa) of the Fe(x)Mn11Al1C series, whereas the coarse carbides (18 nm) in the 20% Mn steel give the highest (896 MPa).

Carbide size also sets the work-hardening capacity: shear deformation of the coherent κ-carbides allows dislocations to glide across κ-carbide shear planes, which weakens work hardening; large carbides therefore correlate with low work-hardening rate and low uniform elongation, and fine carbides (as in Mn-35) correlate with the highest work-hardening rate (~2300 MPa) and highest ductility (60% uniform / 75% total elongation).

The size dependence extends to toughness: Charpy impact energy at −40 °C falls with the square root of κ-carbide size, so the finest-carbide Mn-35 steel retains a higher impact toughness (19.3 J) than the coarser-carbide, lower-Mn/ higher-C grades, whose toughness can collapse to a few joules.

Work-hardening behaviour of most steels shows a typical decline–rise–decline sequence with true strain, whereas the 35% Mn (and 0.6% C) steels show a monotonic decrease of work-hardening rate with increasing true strain.

The near-constant maximum true stress (σ_TS ≈ 1350 MPa) and fracture strength (σ_FS ≈ 2150 MPa) across all compositions — including Mn-35 at 1313 and 2200 MPa — are independent of alloying content and microstructure and are attributed to a microstructural evolution not explained by κ-carbide size alone, flagged as a topic for further study.
conclusions: Within the Fe(x)Mn11Al1C series solution-treated at 1050 °C for 2 h + WQ, the Mn-35 grade (Fe34.23Mn11.10Al1.00C) represents the high-Mn end of the design window: it is single-phase austenite (no ferrite), with the coarsest austenite grains (33 μm), ~60% Σ3 twin boundaries and the finest κ-carbides (2 nm). It is consequently the softest grade (YS 401 MPa, UTS 849 MPa) but the most ductile (UE 60%, A 75.0%) and possesses the highest work-hardening rate (~2300 MPa) of the Mn series, while retaining a modest Charpy impact energy at −40 °C (19.3 J). Its density of 6.53 g/cm³ makes it among the lightest of the studied steels. The sample illustrates the central finding of the study: strength, ductility and impact toughness of solution-treated low-density Fe–Mn–Al–C steels are controlled mainly by the size of the κ-carbides (which set the yield strength through a particle-shear mechanism, YS = 478 + 97.1 d_Car^0.5), rather than by austenite grain size, ferrite fraction or twin-boundary fraction. This positions Mn content as a lever for tuning κ-carbide size and hence the strength–ductility–toughness balance, and supports the broader conclusion that compositional design of low-density steels should aim to control κ-carbide size to avoid the toughness collapse seen in low-C/low-Mn and high-C/high-Al grades.
unmapped: The paper's alloy-density relation ρ = 8.1 − 0.102C − 0.10Al − 0.01Mn (mass%) was fitted over the full 13-alloy set; its Al and Mn coefficients agree with earlier reports (~0.101 and ~0.0085 g/cm³ per mass%), but the C coefficient (0.102 g/cm³ per 1% C) is much smaller than the previously reported 0.41 g/cm³ per 1% C, a discrepancy the authors say materially affects density predictions.

The reference composition Fe30Mn11Al1C appears three times in the composition matrix (as C-1.0, Mn-30 and Al-11) with identical measured properties (UTS 850 ± 4 MPa, YS 688 ± 2 MPa, UE 62 ± 1.3%, A 70.5 ± 1%, Akv-40 98.0 ± 7.1 J, σ_TS 1343 MPa, σ_FS 2095 MPa); Mn-35 lies adjacent to this reference composition in the Mn series and shares the C = 1.0, Al = 11 nominal base.

The stress-strain jumps observed after yielding in the tensile curves were caused by removal of the extensometer to permit testing to high plastic strain and are stated not to affect the property measurements or work-hardening-rate calculations.
